newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Hanbo failure seen aiding S.Korean financial reform.
newsitem.headline: Hanbo failure seen aiding S.Korean financial reform.

text.p: The collapse of South Korea's Hanbo Steel highlights problems caused by industrial conglomerates obsessed with size over profits, but it could speed financial reform, analysts said on Tuesday.
The country's second largest steelmaker borrowed $5.8 billion, mainly to finance a new steel mill that would have turned it into one of the world's biggest producers.
"Management minds are set on sales growth," said Jon Chong-hwa, an analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities. "It's important for them to show off by outsizing the other conglomerates."
In Hanbo's case, the strategy led to ruin.
"Hanbo's investment made no sense," said Rhee Namuh, research head at Dongbang Peregrine Securities. "Completion of the plant would not have generated satisfactory returns."
On Tuesday, police raided the home and office of Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo to try to find out why banks lent massive sums to a project that was arguably a white elephant.

Opposition parties allege that government influence-peddling was behind loans that have plunged financial markets in crisis and led to the biggest financial scandal in President Kim Young-sam's term in office.
Chung was one of the leading patriachs of South Korea's family-run "chaebol", the business conglomerates that dominate the economy.
Personal rivalry between chaebol heads partly explains their blind desire to expand their empires into diverse areas, according to analysts.
Banks have often been unwilling backers of reckless expansion, forced to extend loans by governments that have treated them as state cashiers.
Shipbuilders, for instance, suffered huge losses in the 1980s as a result of over-expansion. Daewoo Group had to be bailed out by the government.
Analysts said the government may now be less willing to step in and save chaebol from their folly.
"Before, people thought chaebols could not go bankrupt, but it's happening," said an analyst at a local brokerage. "Now we can see bigger conglomerates may go bankrupt."
Business conglomerates such as Hanwha, Ssangyong and Daewoo are heavily indebted.
Richard Samuelson, head of research at SBC Warburg, said when big conglomerates ran into trouble, banks were forced to extend "faulty loans under faulty circumstances".
Hanbo Steel borrowed 20 times its net worth. Rhee of Dongbang Peregrine said with that level of exposure, Hanbo was counting on its bankers being unwilling to let it fail.
"Chaebols take advantage of their relationship with local banks that already have large exposure to them," said Rhee.
Now, analysts said the debacle at Hanbo Steel could advance the financial restructuring that President Kim has promised before his term expires in December.

"Hanbo's default could speed up financial reforms," said Kim Sung-soo, an analyst at Hyundai Securities. "By revealing the weak financial structure of these banks, it will hasten mergers in the industry."
Mergers are widely seen as an inevitable consequence of a shake-up in the inefficient banking system.

Analysts said the government was in a quandry over how to handle the Hanbo failure. Unless it gave financial incentives to would-be saviours, nobody would be interested in buying an ailing steel company.
But such concessions would be at odds with the open economy required by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), which Seoul joined last year.
"The government will be under a lot of pressure from the OECD not to do it," said Rhee. "It will not be an easy decision for the government."
